title: Controlling Atom Array in an Ultra-high-cooperativity Optical Cavity
authors: Jilai Ye, Zhihao Chi, Ye Tian, Shuyao Mei, Xiaoyu Li, Wenjun Zhang, Yajuan Zhao, Jiazhong Hu, Wenlan Chen
abstract: Neutral-atom array and cavity quantum electrodynamics offer complementary strengths for quantum science: scalable, reconfigurable qubit architectures and strong coherent light-matter coupling. Combining them in a single platform requires an optical cavity with simultaneously high cooperativity, sufficient mode volume to accommodate atom array, and ample side optical access for atom trapping, imaging, cooling, and rearrangement, a combination that is challenging to achieve. Here we realize an atomic array integrated with a millimeter-scale Fabry--Pérot cavity whose optically-characterized single-atom cooperativity reaches $η_{\mathrm{cav}}=125\pm13$. Atom-cavity transmission spectra of trapped atoms yield an effective spectroscopic cooperativity $η_{\mathrm{spec}}=112.3\pm3.3$, providing an in-situ verification of strong coupling in the integrated platform, and we demonstrate simultaneous coupling of up to 16 individually trapped atoms to the antinode of the cavity mode. The key technical advance is a two-step mirror-fabrication method combining precision mechanical shaping and carbon-dioxide laser polishing, which produces concave fused-silica mirrors with sub-millimeter radii of curvature and residual roughness below 2 Å. Our results establish a regime of cavity-integrated atomic array that simultaneously provides high cooperativity, large mode volume, and flexible manipulation of individual atoms, opening opportunities for cavity-assisted quantum state readout and long-range entanglement-engineering in atom-array platforms.
summary: The research reports the creation of an integrated platform combining neutral-atom arrays with an ultra-high-cooperativity optical cavity. By developing advanced mirror fabrication techniques, they achieved a high cooperativity regime while retaining large mode volume and the ability to trap many individual atoms. This opens pathways for complex quantum state manipulation in solid-state or chip-scale quantum simulators.
main_problem: The challenge is integrating neutral-atom arrays, which provide scalable qubit architectures, with high-cooperativity optical cavities for strong light-matter coupling into a single platform.
main_result: The authors successfully realized an integrated system achieving high cooperativity ($\eta_{	ext{cav}} = 125 \pm 13$) while maintaining large mode volume and the ability to couple up to 16 individually trapped atoms.
method: They employed a two-step mirror fabrication method (mechanical shaping + CO2 laser polishing) to create high-quality, concave fused-silica mirrors for the cavity. Atom coupling was verified by measuring transmission spectra as a function of the number of trapped atoms.
model_or_system: The platform consists of an atomic array coupled to a millimeter-scale Fabry-Pérot optical cavity. Atoms are trapped in an intracavity lattice, allowing controlled interaction with the cavity mode.
key_observables: Single-atom cooperativity ($\eta_{	ext{cav}}$), effective spectroscopic cooperativity ($\eta_{	ext{spec}}$), and cavity transmission spectra as a function of coupled atoms ($N$).
important_parameters: High cooperativity regime ($\eta_{	ext{cav}} = 125 \pm 13$); millimeter-scale cavity length; sub-2 Å mirror roughness.
main_assumptions: The primary comparison is between the ideal single-atom cooperativity ($\eta_{	ext{cav}}$) and the measured in-situ value ($\eta_{	ext{spec}}$), with discrepancies attributed to atomic positioning errors or finite temperature effects.
figures_summary: Figure 2 characterizes the cavity resonance (high finesse, specific linewidth $\kappa$). Figure 3 shows the atom-cavity transmission spectra, demonstrating the collective response as more atoms are added.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the technical challenge of combining large mode volume for arrays with high cooperativity. It then details the advanced mirror fabrication technique enabling the cavity. Finally, it presents spectroscopic measurements confirming strong coupling and scalability up to 16 atoms.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a major engineering hurdle in quantum simulation: building scalable platforms that maintain strong light-matter interaction necessary for complex quantum protocols like entanglement generation or readout.
